subsystems.name: Core Framework
subsystems.description: Core Framework contains the request- and application lifecycle primitives shared by every Flask project: configuration handling, blueprint/scaffold registration, context globals, template loading, helper functions, logging, signals, typing aliases, and class-based views. It is separated from Runtime Support so that the routing/template/context model can be designed and tested without being coupled to a concrete WSGI server, JSON/session cookie mechanics, or the command-line wrapper; this keeps the executable Flask version thin and the underlying sansio abstractions reusable. Data flows from the user's app object into these modules: route decorators defined by `Scaffold.add_url_rule` (`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:376`) record rules, blueprint callbacks are accumulated through `Blueprint.record` and `Blueprint.register`, and contexts created as `AppContext` (`src/flask/ctx.py:260`) keep request and app state on a stack for the `globals.py` proxies to read. `Config` objects with methods such as `from_prefixed_env` and `from_pyfile` supply settings, while `DispatchingJinjaLoader` (`src/flask/templating.py:49`) resolves templates according to app and blueprint loaders. The neighbouring Runtime Support modules (`src/flask/app.py`, `src/flask/cli.py`, `src/flask/sessions.py`, and the JSON/testing files) import and combine these primitives to form the fully executable framework that the example applications and test suite use.

## Overview
`src/flask/blueprints.py` defines the public `Blueprint` class (`src/flask/blueprints.py:18`) that applications use to group routes and templates. It layers filesystem and static-file behavior on top of the pure registration machinery in `src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py`, producing a class that can be registered with an app and then serve its own static resources.

## Why it exists
A Flask blueprint has two distinct responsibilities. Registration state, deferred functions, and URL-rule recording can be described without any request/response I/O; that half lives in the sansio base constructor (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:41`), `add_url_rule` (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:87`), and `record` (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:224`). Serving static files and opening package resources, however, requires Werkzeug response helpers and filesystem access. Keeping those methods here means the sansio blueprint remains importable and testable in contexts that do not need I/O.

## How it works
The concrete `Blueprint.__init__` (`src/flask/blueprints.py:19`) accepts the usual blueprint metadata, resolves the blueprint root path, and initializes the inherited sansio state. Because a blueprint is not yet attached to an app at construction time, route registration work is deferred rather than executed immediately; the base class stores those deferred calls until the blueprint is registered.

The I/O-specific additions begin with `get_send_file_max_age` (`src/flask/blueprints.py:55`), which supplies the cache-age policy that should be used when serving static content. `send_static_file` (`src/flask/blueprints.py:82`) is the method that actually serves a file from the blueprint’s static folder; it resolves the requested filename and uses the helper functions imported by this module to produce a file response. `open_resource` (`src/flask/blueprints.py:104`) provides a lower-level operation: it opens an arbitrary resource relative to the blueprint’s root path and returns a file object, which is useful for templates, text assets, or embedded data.

In normal use, an application registers a blueprint and the deferred rules from the sansio base are replayed against the app; once the app is serving requests, `send_static_file` and `open_resource` carry out any per-file work. This split makes the public `Blueprint` class the complete, usable object while keeping the no-I/O portion small and dependency-light.

## Key symbols
- `Blueprint` (`src/flask/blueprints.py:18`): public blueprint class combining registration and static serving.
- `Blueprint.__init__` (`src/flask/blueprints.py:19`): sets blueprint metadata and defers to the sansio base.
- `get_send_file_max_age` (`src/flask/blueprints.py:55`): computes cache max age for blueprint static files.
- `send_static_file` (`src/flask/blueprints.py:82`): serves a file from the blueprint static folder.
- `open_resource` (`src/flask/blueprints.py:104`): opens a file relative to the blueprint root.

## Overview
`src/flask/config.py` provides two cooperating pieces. `Config` (`src/flask/config.py:50`) is a dict-like holder for all Flask settings, and `ConfigAttribute` (`src/flask/config.py:20`) is a descriptor that maps attributes on an application object to entries in that holder.

## Why it exists
Configuration loading involves several distinct sources: environment variables, Python files, Python objects, and generic file loaders. Keeping that logic in `Config` prevents the application class from accumulating file-parsing details, while `ConfigAttribute` lets application code write `app.secret_key = ...` without exposing `config` bookkeeping at every call site. The file is a separate module so it can be imported independently and so all configuration concerns have one home.

## How it works
`ConfigAttribute.__get__` (`src/flask/config.py:30`) and `__set__` (`src/flask/config.py:46`) implement the descriptor protocol: reading an attribute retrieves a value from the bound object’s config map, and assigning to it writes through to that map. `Config.__init__` (`src/flask/config.py:94`) establishes the initial defaults and remembers the root path used later for file lookup.

The class’s loading methods are the main entry points. `from_envvar` (`src/flask/config.py:102`) reads the name of a configuration file from an environment variable and hands it to `from_pyfile` (`src/flask/config.py:187`), which executes a Python file as configuration. `from_prefixed_env` (`src/flask/config.py:126`) absorbs environment variables sharing a prefix and writes them into config. `from_object` (`src/flask/config.py:218`) takes an object or importable module and copies its configuration attributes. `from_file` (`src/flask/config.py:256`) is the generic variant that accepts a loader function for formats such as JSON or TOML, while `from_mapping` (`src/flask/config.py:304`) merges an existing mapping. Finally, `get_namespace` (`src/flask/config.py:323`) collects every config key under a shared prefix, strips that prefix, and returns the remainder; it is how grouped settings such as `MAIL_*` or `SESSION_*` are read out.

The Flask application object created in `src/flask/sansio/app.py:279` owns one of these `Config` instances and uses `ConfigAttribute` descriptors for its public convenience attributes.

## Key symbols
- `Config` (`src/flask/config.py:50`): stores configuration values and provides all loading methods.
- `ConfigAttribute` (`src/flask/config.py:20`): descriptor translating attribute access into config access.
- `from_pyfile` (`src/flask/config.py:187`): loads config by executing a Python file.
- `from_prefixed_env` (`src/flask/config.py:126`): loads config from prefixed environment variables.
- `from_object` (`src/flask/config.py:218`): copies settings from an object or module.
- `get_namespace` (`src/flask/config.py:323`): returns keys sharing a common prefix.

## Gotchas
When using `from_object`, only uppercase attribute names are copied into the configuration; lowercase module locals used during import are intentionally ignored.

## Overview

`ctx.py` implements the context machinery that makes global proxies such as `g`, `request`, and `session` resolve to per-request state. It defines the dict-like `_AppCtxGlobals` object (src/flask/ctx.py:30), the app/request context objects, and the module-level helpers used to register per-request callbacks or test whether a context is active.

## Why it exists

Flask code executes with an app and request bound implicitly rather than passed through every call. This file separates that concern from `app.py` and from the proxies in `globals.py`: a context object carries the app, environ-derived request data, and per-context storage, and its `push`/`pop` contract makes the request lifecycle explicit. Putting that lifecycle in its own module keeps `Flask.wsgi_app` focused on dispatch instead of stack management.

## How it works

The request path starts from a WSGI environ: `from_environ` (src/flask/ctx.py:340) creates the context, `match_request` (src/flask/ctx.py:405) binds the URL rule and view arguments, and `push` (src/flask/ctx.py:416) activates it as the current context. `pop` (src/flask/ctx.py:446) is paired with `push`; it releases the context and runs teardown work. `__enter__` (src/flask/ctx.py:506) and `__exit__` (src/flask/ctx.py:510) expose the same operations through `with` blocks. Session state is obtained through `_get_session` (src/flask/ctx.py:381) and exposed via the `session` accessor (src/flask/ctx.py:396).

The `_AppCtxGlobals` class backs the per-app `g` object. Its custom attribute methods `__getattr__` (src/flask/ctx.py:53), `__setattr__` (src/flask/ctx.py:59), and `__delattr__` (src/flask/ctx.py:62) make `g` act like an ordinary object, while `get` (src/flask/ctx.py:68), `pop` (src/flask/ctx.py:79), and `setdefault` (src/flask/ctx.py:93) provide a dict-style API. `after_this_request` (src/flask/ctx.py:118) queues a function to run after the current request's response, and `copy_current_request_context` (src/flask/ctx.py:154) wraps a callback so it can later run while remembering the original context. Finally, `has_request_context` (src/flask/ctx.py:209) and `has_app_context` (src/flask/ctx.py:235) provide the cheap guard checks used throughout Flask before touching context-dependent objects.

## Key symbols

- `_AppCtxGlobals` (src/flask/ctx.py:30): the `g` container with attribute and mapping access.
- `push` (src/flask/ctx.py:416) / `pop` (src/flask/ctx.py:446): activate and deactivate a context.
- `match_request` (src/flask/ctx.py:405): route matching before dispatch.
- `after_this_request` (src/flask/ctx.py:118): register a callback for the end of the request.
- `copy_current_request_context` (src/flask/ctx.py:154): preserve the active context for later invocation.
- `has_request_context` (src/flask/ctx.py:209) / `has_app_context` (src/flask/ctx.py:235): context-presence checks.

## Overview
debughelpers.py centralizes development diagnostics for failures whose native exception text is misleading: missing file keys on requests that did not use `multipart/form-data`, form submissions that are swallowed by routing redirects, and unsuccessful template loader lookups. It supplies exception subclasses plus utility functions that produce actionable, human-readable reports.

## Why it exists
Request parsing and template loading should not carry the verbose wording of debug messages. `app.py`, `wrappers.py`, and `templating.py` can import small pieces from this file when they want an improved error, while their normal hot paths stay free of explanation-building code. Keeping the helpers together also gives tests one surface for exercising message construction.

## How it works
`UnexpectedUnicodeError` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:17) is a dual `AssertionError` and `UnicodeError` subclass used to mark decoding problems that should be shown as application faults rather than ordinary unicode errors. `DebugFilesKeyError` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:23) subclasses `KeyError`, so usual missing-key handling still works; its `__init__` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:28) receives the request and the missing file name, examines what was actually submitted, and stores a full explanation in `self.msg`, returned by `__str__` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:46). `FormDataRoutingRedirect` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:50) builds its AssertionError message in `__init__` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:57) when a request was redirected instead of being processed.

`attach_enctype_error_multidict` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:81) installs a dynamic per-request subclass, `newcls` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:90), whose `__getitem__` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:91) intercepts a missing key and raises the clearer `DebugFilesKeyError`; ordinary lookups fall through unchanged. For templates, `_dump_loader_info` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:107) formats one loader/source pair into a label, while `explain_template_loading_attempts` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:124) consumes the attempted loader results and emits a formatted list showing which sources were tried and why each failed, to the app logger when a handler is present or to stderr otherwise.

## Key symbols
- `UnexpectedUnicodeError` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:17) - dual exception type for assert-style unicode failures.
- `DebugFilesKeyError` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:23) - improved KeyError raised when a request-file lookup fails.
- `FormDataRoutingRedirect` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:50) - AssertionError explaining a request was redirected.
- `attach_enctype_error_multidict` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:81) and `newcls` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:90) - monkey-patch the request data lookup with a richer missing-key error.
- `_dump_loader_info` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:107) and `explain_template_loading_attempts` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:124) - diagnostics for template discovery.

## Overview

This module is the home of Flask's context-local globals. It defines `app_ctx`, `current_app`, `g`, `request`, and `session` as lazy proxies so application and framework code can refer to request or app state with ordinary module-level names.

## Why it exists

Context state lives on runtime stacks managed by the application and request context machinery. This file is the central binding point: `flask/__init__.py`, `app.py`, `blueprints.py`, `cli.py`, `ctx.py`, `helpers.py`, and `views.py` are all listed as importers. Isolating the proxies here lets every consumer share one implementation and hides stack lookup from callers, so request handling code does not have to pass `current_app` or `request` through every call chain.

## How it works

`ProxyMixin` (src/flask/globals.py:17) declares the required resolve hook, `_get_current_object` (src/flask/globals.py:18). Subclasses specialize which object a proxy resolves to: `AppContextProxy` (src/flask/globals.py:24) targets the active app context, `_AppCtxGlobalsProxy` (src/flask/globals.py:26) targets the per-context data object behind `g`, `RequestProxy` (src/flask/globals.py:28) targets the request, and `SessionMixinProxy` (src/flask/globals.py:30) targets the session, with `FlaskProxy` (src/flask/globals.py:22) covering the app itself. The module then instantiates the public constants: `app_ctx` (src/flask/globals.py:41), `current_app` (src/flask/globals.py:44), `g` (src/flask/globals.py:47), `request` (src/flask/globals.py:57), and `session` (src/flask/globals.py:60). Any attribute read or write on these proxies goes through the generic `__getattr__` at src/flask/globals.py:65, which forwards the operation to the currently resolved underlying object; this is why mutations made through `g` are visible to the current context only.

## Key symbols

- `ProxyMixin` (src/flask/globals.py:17) and `_get_current_object` (src/flask/globals.py:18): base indirection protocol.
- `FlaskProxy` (src/flask/globals.py:22), `AppContextProxy` (src/flask/globals.py:24), `_AppCtxGlobalsProxy` (src/flask/globals.py:26), `RequestProxy` (src/flask/globals.py:28), `SessionMixinProxy` (src/flask/globals.py:30): typed proxy variants.
- `app_ctx` (src/flask/globals.py:41): proxy to the currently pushed app context.
- `current_app` (src/flask/globals.py:44): active application instance.
- `g` (src/flask/globals.py:47): object for storing data scoped to the current context.
- `request` (src/flask/globals.py:57): current request.
- `session` (src/flask/globals.py:60): session bound to that request.
- `__getattr__` (src/flask/globals.py:65): forwards absent attributes to the current object.

## Gotchas

These names are evaluated lazily rather than bound to a value at import time. The same name can resolve to different objects in different request or app contexts, and dereferencing it when no context is pushed will fail, so callers should not cache a resolved value across context boundaries.

## Overview

`helpers.py` holds reusable request-related functions that are not tied to a single route or app object: debug and dotenv flags, response construction, URL and redirect and abort shortcuts, template attribute access, flashed messages, and file sending.

## Why it exists

These are cross-cutting utilities needed by views, the app object, blueprints, the CLI, and the template layer. Keeping them in this module lets several subsystems and user code share one stable import surface while keeping stateful response and context logic out of `app.py` and `ctx.py`.

## How it works

The configuration helpers `get_debug_flag` (src/flask/helpers.py:28) and `get_load_dotenv` (src/flask/helpers.py:36) translate environment settings into booleans. `stream_with_context` (src/flask/helpers.py:52) supports both a generator and a generator-producing function; when given a callable it returns the wrapper produced by `decorator` (src/flask/helpers.py:120), whose inner `generator` (src/flask/helpers.py:126) preserves the active context while streaming. `make_response` (src/flask/helpers.py:151) normalizes a view return value into a response. `url_for` (src/flask/helpers.py:200) builds URLs, `redirect` (src/flask/helpers.py:254) returns a redirect response, `abort` (src/flask/helpers.py:281) raises an HTTP error directly, and `get_template_attribute` (src/flask/helpers.py:304) exposes a template-level callable to Python. Flashing is handled by `flash` (src/flask/helpers.py:326) to write a message and `get_flashed_messages` (src/flask/helpers.py:360) to read it back. For static files, `_prepare_send_file_kwargs` (src/flask/helpers.py:402) assembles options, `send_file` (src/flask/helpers.py:417) serves one file, and `send_from_directory` (src/flask/helpers.py:543) restricts sending to a directory; `get_root_path` (src/flask/helpers.py:587) and `_split_blueprint_path` (src/flask/helpers.py:645) help resolve package roots and blueprint static prefixes. Finally, `_CollectErrors` (src/flask/helpers.py:654) is an internal context manager whose `__enter__` (src/flask/helpers.py:662) opens a block, `__exit__` (src/flask/helpers.py:665) collects errors, and `raise_any` (src/flask/helpers.py:676) re-raises them after the block if any were recorded.

## Key symbols

- `get_debug_flag` (src/flask/helpers.py:28): reads the debug flag from the environment.
- `get_load_dotenv` (src/flask/helpers.py:36): decides whether to load dotenv files.
- `stream_with_context` (src/flask/helpers.py:52): preserves the request context around a streaming response.
- `make_response` (src/flask/helpers.py:151): converts a view return value into a response.
- `url_for` (src/flask/helpers.py:200), `redirect` (src/flask/helpers.py:254), `abort` (src/flask/helpers.py:281): common view-facing helpers.
- `flash` (src/flask/helpers.py:326) and `get_flashed_messages` (src/flask/helpers.py:360): message queue backed by the session.
- `send_file` (src/flask/helpers.py:417) and `send_from_directory` (src/flask/helpers.py:543): file response helpers.
- `_CollectErrors` (src/flask/helpers.py:654): internal error-recording context manager.

## Overview
logging.py gives each Flask application a usable Python `logging.Logger` without requiring application code to configure logging first, and exposes the WSGI error stream for handlers. It is the implementation behind the application-level `logger` property.

## Why it exists
Logger setup is needed lazily by the application object, but the implementation also needs request-context globals for the error-stream proxy and should not be embedded in `sansio/app.py`. Keeping it separate lets `sansio/app.py` import `create_logger` without creating a circular dependency through request globals, and leaves tests a small, independent module to reset and reconfigure.

## How it works
The `logger` property on the sansio app (src/flask/sansio/app.py:440) delegates to `create_logger` (src/flask/logging.py:58). That function obtains the logger for the app, checks whether a handler already exists via `has_level_handler` (src/flask/logging.py:31), and attaches the module-level `default_handler` (src/flask/logging.py:52), a stderr `StreamHandler`, only when none is present. `has_level_handler` walks up from the app logger through parent loggers, comparing handler levels with the effective level and stopping early when propagation is disabled, so Flask does not install a second handler when an application or test has already configured the logging tree.

For server-side error output, `wsgi_errors_stream` (src/flask/logging.py:16) is a request-scoped proxy that resolves to `request.environ['wsgi.errors']`; it is appropriate for WSGI middleware and request handlers that want to write diagnostics to the server's own error stream.

## Key symbols
- `wsgi_errors_stream` (src/flask/logging.py:16) - request-bound proxy for the active `wsgi.errors` stream.
- `has_level_handler` (src/flask/logging.py:31) - walks the logger hierarchy to decide whether any handler can emit.
- `default_handler` (src/flask/logging.py:52) - shared stderr stream handler with Flask's default formatting.
- `create_logger` (src/flask/logging.py:58) - builds and configures the per-app logger.

## Gotchas
`default_handler` is shared, not copied per app. `create_logger` only adds it when `has_level_handler` reports no capable handler anywhere in the propagation chain, so if a root logger is configured, Flask uses that existing configuration instead of its own stderr format. Also, `wsgi_errors_stream` is only meaningful inside a request context; outside one, accessing the proxy raises the usual context error.

## Overview
`App` (`src/flask/sansio/app.py:59`) is the I/O-independent Flask application object. It owns configuration, URL rules, blueprint registration, template environment helpers, error handling, URL building hooks, and application-context teardown, so the WSGI-facing layer can stay thin. The class is the protocol-neutral core that a server-specific Flask subclass extends.

## Why it exists
Keeping application setup separate from request transport is a deliberate boundary. Routing, template registration, and lifecycle callbacks do not need to know whether the next layer is WSGI, ASGI, or a test client. Putting that shared logic in this file means the subclass in `src/flask/app.py` only has to add context handling and dispatch behavior.

## How it works
Initialization begins in `__init__` (`src/flask/sansio/app.py:279`), which sets up the core state; later setup actions are guarded by `_check_setup_finished` (`410`). Several lazily evaluated properties expose app-wide objects: `name` (`423`), `logger` (`440`), and `jinja_env` (`467`). Configuration is produced through `make_config` (`479`) using `auto_find_instance_path` (`507`) to calculate the instance folder. The `debug` getter (`550`) and setter (`563`) mediate debug mode. URL and blueprint registration happen through `register_blueprint` (`570`) and `add_url_rule` (`605`). Template filters, tests, and globals are added via `add_template_filter` (`699`), `add_template_test` (`756`), and `add_template_global` (`810`), while `create_jinja_environment` (`476`) provides the Jinja environment hook. App-context teardown is registered by `teardown_appcontext` (`827`) and shell variables by `shell_context_processor` (`858`). Error handling starts with `_find_error_handler` (`868`), whose behavior is influenced by `trap_http_exception` (`893`). URL building is supplemented by `inject_url_defaults` (`960`) and error recovery in `handle_url_build_error` (`981`); `redirect` (`939`) builds response-ready redirects.

## Key symbols
- `App` (`src/flask/sansio/app.py:59`): the base application class used by server-specific subclasses.
- `__init__` (`279`): initializes configuration, logging, Jinja, and registries.
- `register_blueprint` (`570`) / `add_url_rule` (`605`): primary extension and routing entry points.
- `add_template_filter` (`699`) / `add_template_test` (`756`) / `add_template_global` (`810`): populate the template environment.
- `_find_error_handler` (`868`) / `trap_http_exception` (`893`): locate and gate exception handlers.
- `inject_url_defaults` (`960`) / `handle_url_build_error` (`981`): support URL generation and report failures.

## Gotchas
Most registration methods assume the application has not started serving. `_check_setup_finished` (`410`) protects that invariant, so changing routes, blueprints, or handlers after the app has begun handling requests raises an error. This `App` is separate from request/response classes; it prepares state, not I/O.

## Overview
This file implements the deferred registration system for Flask blueprints. `BlueprintSetupState` (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:34`) represents the app-bound state used while a blueprint is applied, and `Blueprint` (`119`) collects routes, templates, and hooks so they can be installed onto one or more applications later.

## Why it exists
A blueprint is imported before the application it will be attached to exists, so it cannot call `app.add_url_rule` at definition time. Blueprints therefore record closures and replay them when an app registers them. This separation lets blueprint definitions be reusable, nestable, and independent of any concrete Flask application instance.

## How it works
`Blueprint.__init__` (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:174`) initializes the deferred callback list. Public setup methods do not mutate an app immediately; for example, `Blueprint.add_url_rule` (`413`) stores a callback that will later run against a real app. `record` (`224`) is the ordinary path for appending such callbacks, while `record_once` (`233`) wraps a callback so it is not applied repeatedly. When registration starts, `register` (`273`) is invoked; it checks that setup can still occur via `_check_setup_finished` (`213`), creates a fresh `BlueprintSetupState` through `make_setup_state` (`246`), and replays the recorded functions against that state. The state object's own `add_url_rule` (`87`) is the method that actually applies a rule once the blueprint has access to the target application. Nested blueprints are supported through `register_blueprint` (`256`). After the core deferred functions run, `_merge_blueprint_funcs` (`379`) and `extend` (`380`) consolidate accumulated blueprint-wide functions. App-wide additions are exposed through methods such as `app_template_filter` (`450`), `app_template_test` (`504`), `app_template_global` (`562`), `before_app_request` (`614`), `after_app_request` (`624`), `teardown_app_request` (`634`), `app_context_processor` (`644`), `app_errorhandler` (`656`), `app_url_value_preprocessor` (`673`), and `app_url_defaults` (`685`).

## Key symbols
- `BlueprintSetupState` (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:34`): carries the app and options while deferred functions execute.
- `Blueprint` (`119`): the public blueprint object users import and configure.
- `record` (`224`) / `record_once` (`233`): the queueing mechanism for deferred work.
- `register` (`273`): replays queued work against an app.
- `make_setup_state` (`246`): creates the state passed into each deferred function.

## Gotchas
There are two `add_url_rule` methods. The `Blueprint` one (`413`) queues work; the `BlueprintSetupState` one (`87`) performs the actual install and is only meaningful while registration is running. Treating the blueprint method as an immediate app registration will hide the deferred nature of blueprints.

## Overview
`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py` houses `Scaffold` (`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:52`), the shared, I/O-free base type behind both Flask applications and blueprints. It holds the common registration surface for static files, URL rules, request lifecycle hooks, template context, and error handlers, while concrete subclasses fill in application/blueprint behavior.

## Why it exists
`Flask` and `Blueprint` used to duplicate registration bookkeeping, and both need the same method set before any request/response is involved. Lifting that machinery into this sansio module lets it be implemented and tested once: the application constructor in `src/flask/sansio/app.py:279` and the blueprint constructor in `src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:41` both build on `Scaffold`, and blueprint deferral can use the shared records without touching I/O (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:224`).

## How it works
`setupmethod` (`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:42`) is the guard applied to registration methods. ## Overview

This module declares the canonical signal objects used across Flask. Applications and extensions subscribe to these names to observe lifecycle events such as template rendering, request handling, application-context changes, and flashed messages.

## Why it exists

A single importable namespace prevents each subsystem from creating its own ad-hoc signal objects and lets request, app, template, and helper code refer to the same instances. Keeping the declarations separate from both the code that emits and the code that subscribes gives the framework a small, stable extension surface.

## How it works

The module is intentionally declarative: each constant from line 8 through line 17 is a signal instance rather than a function. The lifecycle is split into groups. `before_render_template` (src/flask/signals.py:9) fires before a template is rendered and `template_rendered` (src/flask/signals.py:8) fires after it, allowing subscribers to inspect or alter the template context. Request lifecycle signals are `request_started` (src/flask/signals.py:10), `request_finished` (src/flask/signals.py:11), `request_tearing_down` (src/flask/signals.py:12), and `got_request_exception` (src/flask/signals.py:13); the last is sent when a view or related code raises. Application-context events are represented by `appcontext_tearing_down` (src/flask/signals.py:14), `appcontext_pushed` (src/flask/signals.py:15), and `appcontext_popped` (src/flask/signals.py:16). Finally, `message_flashed` (src/flask/signals.py:17) is emitted when the `flash` helper queues a message. The importers listed for this module are the internal emitters and exporters: `app.py`, `ctx.py`, `helpers.py`, and `templating.py`, plus the public `flask/__init__.py` package surface. Subscribers connect callbacks to these same objects; because the signals module has no project-local imports, it stays at the bottom of the dependency graph and is safe for any part of the framework to import.

## Key symbols

- `template_rendered` (src/flask/signals.py:8) and `before_render_template` (src/flask/signals.py:9): template rendering hooks.
- `request_started` (src/flask/signals.py:10), `request_finished` (src/flask/signals.py:11), `request_tearing_down` (src/flask/signals.py:12), `got_request_exception` (src/flask/signals.py:13): request lifecycle hooks.
- `appcontext_tearing_down` (src/flask/signals.py:14), `appcontext_pushed` (src/flask/signals.py:15), `appcontext_popped` (src/flask/signals.py:16): application-context lifecycle hooks.
- `message_flashed` (src/flask/signals.py:17): emitted when a message is flashed.

## Gotchas

The order of some declarations differs from the conceptual lifecycle order, so when reading the file it helps to group signals by purpose rather than by line order. These objects are also purely signals for observers; they do not replace return-value conventions or exception handling in the views and context code that emits them.

## Overview

`src/flask/templating.py` adapts Jinja2 to Flask's application and blueprint model and exposes the public rendering helpers that views call. It defines an app-aware Jinja `Environment`, the `DispatchingJinjaLoader` used to locate templates, and functions for normal and streaming template rendering.

## Why it exists

Template handling is a distinct concern from routing and WSGI dispatch, so it has its own module rather than being inlined into the `Flask` class. The loader is separated because template source lookup must consider the app's own template folder plus the folders of every blueprint, while also producing useful error messages in debug mode. Module-level render functions give callers a simple API while keeping implementation details inside this file.

## How it works

`_default_template_ctx_processor` (src/flask/templating.py:21) supplies values that should be present in every template context. The `Environment` class (src/flask/templating.py:36) is a small Jinja environment subclass created for an application and configured from that app's settings. Actual template lookup goes through `DispatchingJinjaLoader` (src/flask/templating.py:49). Its `get_source` method (src/flask/templating.py:57) chooses a fast path, `_get_source_fast` (src/flask/templating.py:88), for ordinary resolution, or `_get_source_explained` (src/flask/templating.py:64), which augments loader errors with diagnostics when running in debug mode. Loader iteration is handled by `_iter_loaders` (src/flask/templating.py:98), which walks the app and its blueprints, and `list_templates` (src/flask/templating.py:108) exposes the aggregate template list.

The public rendering functions build on these objects. `render_template` (src/flask/templating.py:136) calls `_render` (src/flask/templating.py:123) to load a named template and evaluate it with the current context. `render_template_string` (src/flask/templating.py:151) works from template source instead of a name. For incremental output, `_stream` (src/flask/templating.py:163) provides the generator implementation, `generate` (src/flask/templating.py:172) is the internal generation step, and the public wrappers `stream_template` (src/flask/templating.py:181) and `stream_template_string` (src/flask/templating.py:200) expose streaming rendering. Because the streaming helpers return generators, their work does not start until the caller consumes the output, which differs from the eager `render_template` path.

## Key symbols

- `_default_template_ctx_processor` (src/flask/templating.py:21): builds the default variables added to every template context.
- `Environment` (src/flask/templating.py:36): app-configured Jinja environment subclass.
- `DispatchingJinjaLoader` (src/flask/templating.py:49): loader that resolves templates from the app and its blueprints.
- `render_template` (src/flask/templating.py:136) / `render_template_string` (src/flask/templating.py:151): eager public renderers.
- `stream_template` (src/flask/templating.py:181) / `stream_template_string` (src/flask/templating.py:200): lazy streaming renderers.

## Overview
`src/flask/typing.py` is the central type vocabulary for Flask decorators and callback signatures. Its aliases describe what views may return, what callback functions receive, and the shapes expected by route, template, teardown, and error handlers. The module contains only type definitions, with no runtime behavior.

## Why it exists
Many Flask modules share the same annotation needs: `App`, `Blueprint`, `Scaffold`, `views`, and request-context objects all need a consistent description of response values and callback callables. Putting those aliases in one file avoids duplicated unions and prevents every decorator from spelling out the same complex type. Because these are plain aliases rather than imports from other Flask modules, they can be shared widely without entangling module dependencies at runtime.

## How it works
The file composes Python typing constructs into named aliases. `ResponseValue` (`src/flask/typing.py:12`) describes items a view may return, while `HeaderValue` (`26`) and `HeadersValue` (`29`) extend that to HTTP header-shaped values. `ResponseReturnValue` (`36`) is the union used in function signatures, and `ResponseClass` (`47`) names the response class expected by generic helpers. Callable aliases encode callback contracts: `AppOrBlueprintKey` (`49`), `AfterRequestCallable` (`50`), `BeforeRequestCallable` (`55`), `ShellContextProcessorCallable` (`59`), `TeardownCallable` (`60`), and `TemplateContextProcessorCallable` (`64`) describe hooks that attach to the application or blueprint lifecycle. Template registration uses `TemplateFilterCallable` (`67`), `TemplateGlobalCallable` (`68`), and `TemplateTestCallable` (`69`). URL handling appears in `URLDefaultCallable` (`70`) and `URLValuePreprocessorCallable` (`71`). Error registration is covered by `ErrorHandlerCallable` (`79`), and the result of decorating a plain function as a view is captured by `RouteCallable` (`84`).

## Key symbols
- `ResponseValue` (`src/flask/typing.py:12`) / `ResponseReturnValue` (`36`): the response type vocabulary.
- `AfterRequestCallable` (`50`) / `BeforeRequestCallable` (`55`) / `TeardownCallable` (`60`): request lifecycle callback contracts.
- `ErrorHandlerCallable` (`79`): signature for exception handlers.
- `RouteCallable` (`84`): signature of functions exposed as route endpoints.

## Gotchas
These names are type aliases, not runtime functions or callables. They are useful to static type checkers and documented annotations, but they cannot be called or used with `isinstance` at runtime.

## Overview
`src/flask/views.py` provides class-based view support. `View` (`src/flask/views.py:16`) is the base class whose subclasses override `dispatch_request`, and `MethodView` (`138`) adds automatic HTTP-method dispatch. Together they give route endpoints an object-oriented alternative to plain functions.

## Why it exists
Flask's route registry expects a callable, not a class, but some applications organize endpoints around classes or need a common base class for shared behavior. This module is the adapter layer between those classes and route registration. It converts a class into a callable and implements the common method-name convention without each view subclass writing its own glue code.

## How it works
A subclass of `View` implements `dispatch_request` (`src/flask/views.py:78`) and is registered through the class method `as_view` (`86`). `as_view` creates a closure function, with inner `view` implementations at `106` and `115`, that is given a name and returned to Flask's URL registry. When a request is routed to that closure, it instantiates the view class and invokes `dispatch_request`, so each request gets an instance of the subclass while the registry still only sees a function.

`MethodView` extends this pattern. `http_method_funcs` (`src/flask/views.py:11`) declares the recognized lowercase HTTP method names. During subclass creation, `__init_subclass__` (`165`) inspects the class body and records which methods are present, so the view advertises only the HTTP methods it can handle. At request time, `MethodView.dispatch_request` (`182`) reads the active request method and calls the matching class attribute such as `get` or `post`.

## Key symbols
- `View` (`src/flask/views.py:16`): base class for single-dispatch class-based views.
- `dispatch_request` (`78`): the method subclasses implement.
- `as_view` (`86`): converts a view class into a routable function.
- `MethodView` (`138`): base class that dispatches to method-named handlers.
- `__init_subclass__` (`165`): computes allowed methods from the subclass definition.
- `dispatch_request` (`182`): routes the current request to `get`, `post`, etc.

## Gotchas
`MethodView`'s allowed methods are decided in `__init_subclass__` (`165`) from the class body. Adding an HTTP handler to an instance after the class has been created will not make that method routable, because the dispatch table was already fixed at class creation.

subsystems.name: Example Applications
subsystems.description: Example Applications is a set of standalone projects that demonstrate Flask usage in realistic, runnable form: a Celery background-task app, a JavaScript fetch demo, and the complete tutorial blog. This subsystem exists separately from the library internals so maintainers can exercise developer-facing patterns - application factories, blueprint composition, teardown cleanup, login helpers, database commands, and async task integration - without mixing tutorial code into `src/flask`. In each example, an application factory such as `create_app` (`examples/tutorial/flaskr/__init__.py:6`) builds the Flask app and registers blueprints; the tutorial's `db.py` adds teardown and shell/CLI hooks, while `auth.py` and `blog.py` use `g`, `session`, and `request` to implement user and post views. The celery example wires Celery to Flask through `FlaskTask` and `celery_init_app` so tasks such as `add`, `block`, and `process` receive an app context. Its JavaScript example is a minimal single-module app whose `index`/`add` views call `fetch`. Together these applications exercise and validate the Core and Runtime subsystems, and the `examples/*/tests` directories show how the same public APIs are consumed from pytest.

subsystems.name: Runtime Support
subsystems.description: Runtime Support turns the Core Framework's sansio primitives into a concrete WSGI web framework by adding the executable `Flask` class, development server launcher, Click CLI, JSON provider stack, signed cookie sessions, testing client, and request/response wrappers. It exists as a separate subsystem so that all low-level environment integration lives in one place while route registration, context management, config, and templating remain protocol-neutral in Core Framework. Control flows through `Flask.wsgi_app` (`src/flask/app.py:1569`), which prepares request and app contexts, dispatches the request, processes the result as a response, and runs teardown hooks; local development starts from `Flask.run` (`src/flask/app.py:633`) or the CLI's `run_command`. JSON responses route through the configurable `JSONProvider`, sessions are opened and saved by `SecureCookieSessionInterface` (`src/flask/sessions.py:284`), and tests exercise the whole stack with `FlaskClient` (`src/flask/testing.py:109`) and `Request`/`Response` (`src/flask/wrappers.py:18`). The subsystem also hosts the Flask CLI machinery and JSON tagged serializer utilities needed by sessions. It connects back to Core Framework and other neighbours by importing `sansio.app.App`, `blueprints`, `ctx`, `globals`, `helpers`, and `templating`, which provide all higher-level APIs used by the example applications.

## Overview

`src/flask/app.py` contains the concrete `Flask` class (src/flask/app.py:110) and the machinery that turns a configured Flask object into a WSGI application. It handles request dispatch, response finalization, exception handling, dev-server execution, static resources, and the hooks that connect the application to session, template, and test utilities.

## Why it exists

Route registration, configuration, and other request-independent bookkeeping live in the sansio app layer; this file adds the parts that depend on WSGI environ objects and HTTP responses. Keeping the concrete `Flask` class separate concentrates the WSGI-specific execution path in one place and lets the sansio base stay usable by code that does not need a full WSGI stack. `src/flask/app.py` is also the file that other modules import when they need the full application class rather than just the I/O-neutral foundation.

## How it works

A WSGI server calls the application object, reaching `__call__` (src/flask/app.py:1621), which delegates to `wsgi_app` (src/flask/app.py:1569). That method wraps a single request in a context obtained from `request_context` (src/flask/app.py:1504), so request and app state exist while the view runs. `full_dispatch_request` (src/flask/app.py:995) is the dispatch orchestrator: `preprocess_request` (src/flask/app.py:1369) runs before-request hooks, `dispatch_request` (src/flask/app.py:969) resolves and invokes the endpoint, and `finalize_request` (src/flask/app.py:1024) converts the view return value into the final response. `process_response` (src/flask/app.py:1397) runs after-request handlers, and the teardown functions `do_teardown_request` (src/flask/app.py:1423) and `do_teardown_appcontext` (src/flask/app.py:1456) clean up request and app state.

Exceptions raised during dispatch funnel through `handle_user_exception` (src/flask/app.py:868), with unhandled failures passed to `handle_exception` (src/flask/app.py:900) and logged through `log_exception` (src/flask/app.py:953). `ensure_sync` (src/flask/app.py:1068) adapts async view functions and handlers so the synchronous dispatch core can invoke them uniformly. Other notable pieces include `make_response` (src/flask/app.py:1227), used to convert handler return values into `Response` objects, and `run` (src/flask/app.py:633), which starts the local development server.

## Key symbols

- `Flask` (src/flask/app.py:110): the application class users instantiate or subclass.
- `__call__` (src/flask/app.py:1621) / `wsgi_app` (src/flask/app.py:1569): request entry points for WSGI servers.
- `full_dispatch_request` (src/flask/app.py:995): coordinates before-request hooks, dispatch, and finalization.
- `handle_user_exception` (src/flask/app.py:868) / `handle_exception` (src/flask/app.py:900): error-to-response conversion paths.
- `process_response` (src/flask/app.py:1397): applies after-request hooks and final response processing.
- `ensure_sync` (src/flask/app.py:1068): bridges async and sync callables.

## Overview

`cli.py` implements the `flask` command-line interface. It locates and loads an application from an import string or file path, adapts Click groups to Flask, and provides the `run`, `shell`, and `routes` subcommands used during development and debugging.

## Why it exists

The CLI has its own discovery logic, command state, and Click integration that would otherwise be mixed into the application object. Keeping it separate lets `app.py` stay focused on HTTP serving while the developer-facing tooling lives behind the `flask` entry point. It also imports the same global and helper modules users import when their app is executed by the server.

## How it works

App discovery is handled before the main `locate_app` implementation at src/flask/cli.py:241, with overload variants at src/flask/cli.py:230 and src/flask/cli.py:236. `find_app_by_string` (src/flask/cli.py:120) parses the `module:name` style import target and uses `find_best_app` (src/flask/cli.py:41) to choose a factory or instance; `_called_with_wrong_args` (src/flask/cli.py:94) detects the common mistake of calling a factory with arguments. `prepare_import` (src/flask/cli.py:200) converts a path into an importable module. On the state side, `ScriptInfo` (src/flask/cli.py:293) stores CLI options in `__init__` (src/flask/cli.py:305) and exposes `load_app` (src/flask/cli.py:333), which is the choke point through which every command obtains the target application. The `with_appcontext` decorator (src/flask/cli.py:380), whose wrapper begins at src/flask/cli.py:395, runs commands with an application context pushed. `FlaskGroup` (src/flask/cli.py:531) is the Click group subclass: its `__init__` (src/flask/cli.py:563) wires app loading, `_load_plugin_commands` (src/flask/cli.py:600) discovers plugin commands, `get_command` (src/flask/cli.py:609) and `list_commands` (src/flask/cli.py:636) expose them, and `make_context` (src/flask/cli.py:657) plus `parse_args` (src/flask/cli.py:678) integrate Flask setup with Click's argument parsing. Dotenv loading happens through `load_dotenv` (src/flask/cli.py:698), and `show_server_banner` (src/flask/cli.py:766) prints the startup banner. The public commands are `run_command` (src/flask/cli.py:935), `shell_command` (src/flask/cli.py:1001), and `routes_command` (src/flask/cli.py:1061). Finally, `cli` (src/flask/cli.py:1110) assembles the default group and `main` (src/flask/cli.py:1122) is the console entry point.

## Key symbols

- `find_best_app` (src/flask/cli.py:41), `find_app_by_string` (src/flask/cli.py:120), `locate_app` (src/flask/cli.py:241): app discovery chain.

- `with_appcontext` (src/flask/cli.py:380): decorator that ensures a command runs inside an app context.

- `cli` (src/flask/cli.py:1110) and `main` (src/flask/cli.py:1122): command registration and entry point.

## Overview

`src/flask/json/__init__.py` is the public JSON facade of Flask. It provides the familiar stdlib-style functions `dumps`, `dump`, `loads`, and `load`, plus `jsonify` for turning data into an HTTP JSON response. The module contains little serialization logic itself; instead it exposes the serialization configured on the active application's JSON provider.

## Why it exists

The package separates provider implementations in `src/flask/json/provider.py` from the public functions users import. Keeping the provider classes there lets serialization behavior be reusable and app-configurable, while this `__init__.py` gives a stable public API and avoids importing the full `Flask` application class. It imports only support modules such as `globals.py`, `wrappers.py`, and the provider, which helps prevent import cycles with `app.py`.

## How it works

The actual encoding and decoding behavior lives on the JSON provider: `dumps` and `dump` in the provider serialize Python objects (src/flask/json/provider.py:41 and src/flask/json/provider.py:49), while `loads` and `load` parse JSON back into Python values (src/flask/json/provider.py:59 and src/flask/json/provider.py:67). The module-level functions are thin adapters around that provider, so a Flask app can customize its JSON behavior by changing or wrapping its configured provider rather than by patching these helpers.

`dumps` (src/flask/json/__init__.py:13) returns a JSON string, and `dump` (src/flask/json/__init__.py:47) writes that serialized value to a file-like object. `loads` (src/flask/json/__init__.py:77) reads a JSON string, while `load` (src/flask/json/__init__.py:108) reads from a file-like object. The remaining public function, `jsonify` (src/flask/json/__init__.py:138), is the response-oriented helper used by view functions: it accepts either keyword arguments or a single positional dict and produces the JSON response object. Its response-preparation work is delegated to the provider path represented by `_prepare_response_obj` (src/flask/json/provider.py:75).

## Key symbols

- `dumps` (src/flask/json/__init__.py:13): serialize a Python object to a JSON string through the current app's provider.
- `dump` (src/flask/json/__init__.py:47): serialize to a writable file-like object.
- `loads` (src/flask/json/__init__.py:77): deserialize JSON from a string.
- `load` (src/flask/json/__init__.py:108): deserialize JSON from a file-like object.
- `jsonify` (src/flask/json/__init__.py:138): create a JSON HTTP response for view returns.

## Overview
The JSON layer in Flask is deliberately swappable. `JSONProvider` (`src/flask/json/provider.py:19`) defines the interface an app uses for serializing, deserializing, and building a JSON response. `DefaultJSONProvider` (`src/flask/json/provider.py:124`) is the stock implementation that ships with Flask and wires JSON settings to the application configuration.

## Why it exists
If applications need a different JSON library, they should not have to replace Flask source code. The provider boundary gives one place to install an alternate encoder/decoder while keeping the same public helpers such as `src/flask/json/__init__.py:13` (`dumps`), `src/flask/json/__init__.py:77` (`loads`), and `src/flask/json/__init__.py:138` (`jsonify`). It also separates low-level text conversion from creating `Response` objects with JSON content.

## How it works
`JSONProvider.__init__` (`src/flask/json/provider.py:38`) takes and stores the owning app, so every provider object is bound to one application’s configuration. `dumps` (`src/flask/json/provider.py:41`) and `loads` (`src/flask/json/provider.py:59`) are the serialization primitives; implementations of `dump` (`src/flask/json/provider.py:49`) and `load` (`src/flask/json/provider.py:67`) reuse them for file-style input/output. Before an object becomes a response, `_prepare_response_obj` (`src/flask/json/provider.py:75`) normalizes it, and the base `response` method (`src/flask/json/provider.py:89`) wraps the JSON text in the app’s response class.

`DefaultJSONProvider` is the class an unmodified Flask app uses. It overrides `dumps` (`src/flask/json/provider.py:166`) with the standard-library encoder plus Flask’s default type handling, overrides `loads` (`src/flask/json/provider.py:181`) symmetrically, and supplies a response implementation (`src/flask/json/provider.py:189`) that produces the common `application/json` response. The module-level `_default` (`src/flask/json/provider.py:108`) acts as the fallback object serializer for values the regular encoder cannot handle.

Applications that want custom behavior choose a provider when constructing the Flask object; the constructor shown in `src/flask/sansio/app.py:279` owns that wiring, while code importing from `src/flask/json/__init__.py` simply forwards to the current app’s provider.

## Overview
`src/flask/json/tag.py` implements the tagged JSON serializer used for data that must survive JSON encoding with extra type information. `TaggedJSONSerializer` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:219`) transforms Python values through registered tags and then converts the tagged form to or from JSON. The module is used by Flask's session machinery so session contents can include values beyond plain strings, numbers, lists, and dictionaries.

## Why it exists
JSON natively handles only a small set of types. Cookies and secure sessions need to round-trip values such as bytes, UUIDs, datetimes, tuples, and Markup objects without silently changing their type. A separate tag layer records type information inside the JSON structure, allowing `dumps` and `loads` to restore the original Python object while the serialized data remains valid JSON.

## How it works
The base tag contract is `JSONTag` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:60`), whose subclasses implement `check`, `to_json`, and `to_python`. Built-in tags cover dictionaries (`TagDict`, `93`), pass-through dictionaries (`PassDict`, `119`), tuples (`TagTuple`, `133`), pass-through lists (`PassList`, `147`), bytes (`TagBytes`, `159`), Markup (`TagMarkup`, `173`), UUIDs (`TagUUID`, `191`), and datetimes (`TagDateTime`, `205`). The `TaggedJSONSerializer` constructor (`249`) starts with these tags, and `register` (`256`) is the extension point for custom tag classes.

Encoding begins with `tag` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:289`), which walks values, asks each tag whether it matches, and nests tagged output. Decoding is the inverse: `untag` (`297`) and the internal `_untag_scan` (`309`) detect tagged markers and call the appropriate `to_python`. Public operations are `dumps` (`321`) and `loads` (`325`), which hand the tagged representation to and from standard JSON.

## Key symbols
- `JSONTag` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:60`): base interface for all tags.
- `TaggedJSONSerializer` (`219`): central registry and recursive encoder/decoder.
- `register` (`256`): adds or replaces a tag class.
- `tag` (`289`) / `untag` (`297`): recursive conversion between Python objects and tagged JSON.
- `dumps` (`321`) / `loads` (`325`): public JSON-facing wrappers.

## Gotchas
The tag and untag transformations are paired. Each built-in tag has matching `to_json` and `to_python` methods, and changing one side without the other will make previously serialized session data unreadable. Custom tags registered through `register` (`256`) must also implement both directions for full round-tripping.

## Overview
`src/flask/sessions.py` is Flask's cookie-session layer. It provides dict-like session objects and the interfaces Flask uses to load a session from a request cookie and serialize changes back into a response cookie.

## Why it exists
The file separates dictionary-like session state from Flask's stateless HTTP transport. All generic cookie/expiration policy is confined to `SessionInterface` (src/flask/sessions.py:100), while `NullSession` (src/flask/sessions.py:83) provides a sentinel for contexts where no real session should be written, and `SecureCookieSessionInterface` (src/flask/sessions.py:284) contains the default signed-cookie implementation. Because these responsibilities are isolated here, an application can replace its session backend without changing request handling in `app.py`, `ctx.py`, or `wrappers.py`.

## How it works
`SessionMixin` (src/flask/sessions.py:24) adds Flask session semantics to a mapping. The `permanent` accessors at src/flask/sessions.py:28 and src/flask/sessions.py:33 expose the `permanent` flag, storing it as `_permanent` in the underlying mapping. `SecureCookieSession` (src/flask/sessions.py:57) is the concrete in-memory session container; its `__init__` at src/flask/sessions.py:73 wires `on_update` (src/flask/sessions.py:77) so mutations mark the session as changed. `NullSession` (src/flask/sessions.py:83) stands in when a real session cannot exist, with `_fail` (src/flask/sessions.py:89) rejecting operations on the disabled session.

`SessionInterface` (src/flask/sessions.py:100) handles policy that is independent of transport. `make_null_session` and `is_null_session` (src/flask/sessions.py:150 and src/flask/sessions.py:162) define how the null sentinel is created and recognized. The `get_cookie_*` methods read cookie attributes from app configuration: name at src/flask/sessions.py:171, domain at src/flask/sessions.py:175, path at src/flask/sessions.py:187, httponly at src/flask/sessions.py:195, secure at src/flask/sessions.py:202, samesite at src/flask/sessions.py:208, and partitioned at src/flask/sessions.py:215. `get_expiration_time` (src/flask/sessions.py:223) and `should_set_cookie` (src/flask/sessions.py:233) determine whether, and with what lifetime, a cookie should be emitted or refreshed. `open_session` and `save_session` at src/flask/sessions.py:249 and src/flask/sessions.py:263 are the hooks subclass interfaces implement.

The default backend, `SecureCookieSessionInterface` (src/flask/sessions.py:284), uses the shared `session_json_serializer` (src/flask/sessions.py:273) and the digest helper `_lazy_sha1` (src/flask/sessions.py:276) to build a signing serializer in `get_signing_serializer` (src/flask/sessions.py:303). Its `open_session` (src/flask/sessions.py:323) verifies and loads the incoming cookie into a session object; `save_session` (src/flask/sessions.py:337) serializes the session dictionary and either sets or deletes the `Set-Cookie` header.

## Key symbols
- `SessionMixin` (src/flask/sessions.py:24) — adds session attributes to a mapping; permanent-flag accessors at src/flask/sessions.py:28 and src/flask/sessions.py:33.

- `NullSession` (src/flask/sessions.py:83) — sentinel session whose `_fail` method (src/flask/sessions.py:89) rejects use.
- `SessionInterface` (src/flask/sessions.py:100) — generic cookie policy and open/save contract.
- `SecureCookieSessionInterface` (src/flask/sessions.py:284) — default signed-cookie backend; serializer creation at src/flask/sessions.py:303, open/save at src/flask/sessions.py:323 and src/flask/sessions.py:337.

## Overview

`wrappers.py` defines Flask's `Request` and `Response` classes. They extend the generic WSGI request and response types with Flask-specific routing metadata, body-size behavior, JSON-error handling, and cookie-size configuration.

## Why it exists

The underlying WSGI types deliberately know nothing about Flask application configuration or URL rules. This file is the adaptation layer: route information and per-request limits can only be expressed correctly once the active application and context are known. Because the classes are defined here, they can be imported indirectly by `app.py`, `ctx.py`, `globals.py`, `blueprints.py`, and other modules without embedding WSGI details in those files.

## How it works

The `Request` class starts at src/flask/wrappers.py:18. Several of its settings are implemented as property getter and setter pairs. `max_content_length` appears at the getter on src/flask/wrappers.py:60 and returns on the setter at src/flask/wrappers.py:89; `max_form_memory_size` uses getter at src/flask/wrappers.py:93 and setter at src/flask/wrappers.py:116; `max_form_parts` uses getter at src/flask/wrappers.py:120 and setter at src/flask/wrappers.py:143. These paired accessors let the size limits be resolved when the request is used while still allowing a caller to override them on a particular request. After limits are set up, `_load_form_data` (src/flask/wrappers.py:197) performs the actual form parsing; when JSON parsing fails, `on_json_loading_failed` (src/flask/wrappers.py:212) supplies the error reported to the caller. Routing metadata is exposed by three read-only properties: `endpoint` (src/flask/wrappers.py:147) returns the matched endpoint name, `blueprint` (src/flask/wrappers.py:162) returns the primary blueprint for the match, and `blueprints` (src/flask/wrappers.py:181) returns the full list of matching blueprints. The class is completed by `Request` ending around src/flask/wrappers.py:219.

The `Response` class starts at src/flask/wrappers.py:222. It provides `max_cookie_size` at src/flask/wrappers.py:247, giving Flask-controlled responses a cookie-size cap independent of the Werkzeug default.

## Key symbols

- `Request` (src/flask/wrappers.py:18): Flask-aware request object.
- `max_content_length` (src/flask/wrappers.py:60, setter at 89): request body size cap.
- `max_form_memory_size` (src/flask/wrappers.py:93, setter at 116): form data memory cap.
- `max_form_parts` (src/flask/wrappers.py:120, setter at 143): form part count cap.
- `endpoint` (src/flask/wrappers.py:147), `blueprint` (src/flask/wrappers.py:162), `blueprints` (src/flask/wrappers.py:181): routing metadata.
- `_load_form_data` (src/flask/wrappers.py:197): parses request form data subject to the limits above.
- `on_json_loading_failed` (src/flask/wrappers.py:212): custom JSON parse failure handling.

## Overview

This module is the home of Flask's context-local globals. It defines `app_ctx`, `current_app`, `g`, `request`, and `session` as lazy proxies so application and framework code can refer to request or app state with ordinary module-level names.

## Why it exists

Context state lives on runtime stacks managed by the application and request context machinery. This file is the central binding point: `flask/__init__.py`, `app.py`, `blueprints.py`, `cli.py`, `ctx.py`, `helpers.py`, and `views.py` are all listed as importers. Isolating the proxies here lets every consumer share one implementation and hides stack lookup from callers, so request handling code does not have to pass `current_app` or `request` through every call chain.

## How it works

`ProxyMixin` (src/flask/globals.py:17) declares the required resolve hook, `_get_current_object` (src/flask/globals.py:18). Subclasses specialize which object a proxy resolves to: `AppContextProxy` (src/flask/globals.py:24) targets the active app context, `_AppCtxGlobalsProxy` (src/flask/globals.py:26) targets the per-context data object behind `g`, `RequestProxy` (src/flask/globals.py:28) targets the request, and `SessionMixinProxy` (src/flask/globals.py:30) targets the session, with `FlaskProxy` (src/flask/globals.py:22) covering the app itself. The module then instantiates the public constants: `app_ctx` (src/flask/globals.py:41), `current_app` (src/flask/globals.py:44), `g` (src/flask/globals.py:47), `request` (src/flask/globals.py:57), and `session` (src/flask/globals.py:60). Any attribute read or write on these proxies goes through the generic `__getattr__` at src/flask/globals.py:65, which forwards the operation to the currently resolved underlying object; this is why mutations made through `g` are visible to the current context only.

## Key symbols

- `ProxyMixin` (src/flask/globals.py:17) and `_get_current_object` (src/flask/globals.py:18): base indirection protocol.
- `FlaskProxy` (src/flask/globals.py:22), `AppContextProxy` (src/flask/globals.py:24), `_AppCtxGlobalsProxy` (src/flask/globals.py:26), `RequestProxy` (src/flask/globals.py:28), `SessionMixinProxy` (src/flask/globals.py:30): typed proxy variants.
- `app_ctx` (src/flask/globals.py:41): proxy to the currently pushed app context.
- `current_app` (src/flask/globals.py:44): active application instance.
- `g` (src/flask/globals.py:47): object for storing data scoped to the current context.
- `request` (src/flask/globals.py:57): current request.
- `session` (src/flask/globals.py:60): session bound to that request.
- `__getattr__` (src/flask/globals.py:65): forwards absent attributes to the current object.

## Gotchas

These names are evaluated lazily rather than bound to a value at import time. The same name can resolve to different objects in different request or app contexts, and dereferencing it when no context is pushed will fail, so callers should not cache a resolved value across context boundaries.

## Overview

`helpers.py` holds reusable request-related functions that are not tied to a single route or app object: debug and dotenv flags, response construction, URL and redirect and abort shortcuts, template attribute access, flashed messages, and file sending.

## Why it exists

## Overview

This module declares the canonical signal objects used across Flask. Applications and extensions subscribe to these names to observe lifecycle events such as template rendering, request handling, application-context changes, and flashed messages.

## Why it exists

A single importable namespace prevents each subsystem from creating its own ad-hoc signal objects and lets request, app, template, and helper code refer to the same instances. Keeping the declarations separate from both the code that emits and the code that subscribes gives the framework a small, stable extension surface.

## How it works

The module is intentionally declarative: each constant from line 8 through line 17 is a signal instance rather than a function. The lifecycle is split into groups. `before_render_template` (src/flask/signals.py:9) fires before a template is rendered and `template_rendered` (src/flask/signals.py:8) fires after it, allowing subscribers to inspect or alter the template context. Request lifecycle signals are `request_started` (src/flask/signals.py:10), `request_finished` (src/flask/signals.py:11), `request_tearing_down` (src/flask/signals.py:12), and `got_request_exception` (src/flask/signals.py:13); the last is sent when a view or related code raises. Finally, `message_flashed` (src/flask/signals.py:17) is emitted when the `flash` helper queues a message. ## Overview
The JSON layer in Flask is deliberately swappable. `JSONProvider` (`src/flask/json/provider.py:19`) defines the interface an app uses for serializing, deserializing, and building a JSON response. `DefaultJSONProvider` (`src/flask/json/provider.py:124`) is the stock implementation that ships with Flask and wires JSON settings to the application configuration.

## Why it exists
If applications need a different JSON library, they should not have to replace Flask source code. The provider boundary gives one place to install an alternate encoder/decoder while keeping the same public helpers such as `src/flask/json/__init__.py:13` (`dumps`), `src/flask/json/__init__.py:77` (`loads`), and `src/flask/json/__init__.py:138` (`jsonify`). It also separates low-level text conversion from creating `Response` objects with JSON content.

`JSONProvider.__init__` (`src/flask/json/provider.py:38`) takes and stores the owning app, so every provider object is bound to one application’s configuration. `dumps` (`src/flask/json/provider.py:41`) and `loads` (`src/flask/json/provider.py:59`) are the serialization primitives; implementations of `dump` (`src/flask/json/provider.py:49`) and `load` (`src/flask/json/provider.py:67`) reuse them for file-style input/output. Before an object becomes a response, `_prepare_response_obj` (`src/flask/json/provider.py:75`) normalizes it, and the base `response` method (`src/flask/json/provider.py:89`) wraps the JSON text in the app’s response class.

## Overview
`src/flask/typing.py` is the central type vocabulary for Flask decorators and callback signatures. Its aliases describe what views may return, what callback functions receive, and the shapes expected by route, template, teardown, and error handlers. The module contains only type definitions, with no runtime behavior.

## Why it exists
Many Flask modules share the same annotation needs: `App`, `Blueprint`, `Scaffold`, `views`, and request-context objects all need a consistent description of response values and callback callables. Putting those aliases in one file avoids duplicated unions and prevents every decorator from spelling out the same complex type. Because these are plain aliases rather than imports from other Flask modules, they can be shared widely without entangling module dependencies at runtime.

## How it works
The file composes Python typing constructs into named aliases. `ResponseValue` (`src/flask/typing.py:12`) describes items a view may return, while `HeaderValue` (`26`) and `HeadersValue` (`29`) extend that to HTTP header-shaped values. `ResponseReturnValue` (`36`) is the union used in function signatures, and `ResponseClass` (`47`) names the response class expected by generic helpers. Callable aliases encode callback contracts: `AppOrBlueprintKey` (`49`), `AfterRequestCallable` (`50`), `BeforeRequestCallable` (`55`), `ShellContextProcessorCallable` (`59`), `TeardownCallable` (`60`), and `TemplateContextProcessorCallable` (`64`) describe hooks that attach to the application or blueprint lifecycle. Template registration uses `TemplateFilterCallable` (`67`), `TemplateGlobalCallable` (`68`), and `TemplateTestCallable` (`69`). URL handling appears in `URLDefaultCallable` (`70`) and `URLValuePreprocessorCallable` (`71`). Error registration is covered by `ErrorHandlerCallable` (`79`), and the result of decorating a plain function as a view is captured by `RouteCallable` (`84`).

## Key symbols
- `ResponseValue` (`src/flask/typing.py:12`) / `ResponseReturnValue` (`36`): the response type vocabulary.
- `AfterRequestCallable` (`50`) / `BeforeRequestCallable` (`55`) / `TeardownCallable` (`60`): request lifecycle callback contracts.
- `ErrorHandlerCallable` (`79`): signature for exception handlers.
- `RouteCallable` (`84`): signature of functions exposed as route endpoints.

## Gotchas
These names are type aliases, not runtime functions or callables. They are useful to static type checkers and documented annotations, but they cannot be called or used with `isinstance` at runtime.

## Overview
This file implements the deferred registration system for Flask blueprints. `BlueprintSetupState` (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:34`) represents the app-bound state used while a blueprint is applied, and `Blueprint` (`119`) collects routes, templates, and hooks so they can be installed onto one or more applications later.

## Why it exists
A blueprint is imported before the application it will be attached to exists, so it cannot call `app.add_url_rule` at definition time. Blueprints therefore record closures and replay them when an app registers them. This separation lets blueprint definitions be reusable, nestable, and independent of any concrete Flask application instance.

## How it works
`Blueprint.__init__` (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:174`) initializes the deferred callback list. Public setup methods do not mutate an app immediately; for example, `Blueprint.add_url_rule` (`413`) stores a callback that will later run against a real app. `record` (`224`) is the ordinary path for appending such callbacks, while `record_once` (`233`) wraps a callback so it is not applied repeatedly. When registration starts, `register` (`273`) is invoked; it checks that setup can still occur via `_check_setup_finished` (`213`), creates a fresh `BlueprintSetupState` through `make_setup_state` (`246`), and replays the recorded functions against that state. The state object's own `add_url_rule` (`87`) is the method that actually applies a rule once the blueprint has access to the target application. Nested blueprints are supported through `register_blueprint` (`256`). After the core deferred functions run, `_merge_blueprint_funcs` (`379`) and `extend` (`380`) consolidate accumulated blueprint-wide functions. App-wide additions are exposed through methods such as `app_template_filter` (`450`), `app_template_test` (`504`), `app_template_global` (`562`), `before_app_request` (`614`), `after_app_request` (`624`), `teardown_app_request` (`634`), `app_context_processor` (`644`), `app_errorhandler` (`656`), `app_url_value_preprocessor` (`673`), and `app_url_defaults` (`685`).

## Key symbols
- `BlueprintSetupState` (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:34`): carries the app and options while deferred functions execute.
- `Blueprint` (`119`): the public blueprint object users import and configure.
- `record` (`224`) / `record_once` (`233`): the queueing mechanism for deferred work.
- `register` (`273`): replays queued work against an app.
- `make_setup_state` (`246`): creates the state passed into each deferred function.

## Gotchas
There are two `add_url_rule` methods. The `Blueprint` one (`413`) queues work; the `BlueprintSetupState` one (`87`) performs the actual install and is only meaningful while registration is running. Treating the blueprint method as an immediate app registration will hide the deferred nature of blueprints.

## Overview
`src/flask/views.py` provides class-based view support. `View` (`src/flask/views.py:16`) is the base class whose subclasses override `dispatch_request`, and `MethodView` (`138`) adds automatic HTTP-method dispatch. Together they give route endpoints an object-oriented alternative to plain functions.

## Why it exists
Flask's route registry expects a callable, not a class, but some applications organize endpoints around classes or need a common base class for shared behavior. This module is the adapter layer between those classes and route registration. It converts a class into a callable and implements the common method-name convention without each view subclass writing its own glue code.

## How it works
A subclass of `View` implements `dispatch_request` (`src/flask/views.py:78`) and is registered through the class method `as_view` (`86`). `as_view` creates a closure function, with inner `view` implementations at `106` and `115`, that is given a name and returned to Flask's URL registry. When a request is routed to that closure, it instantiates the view class and invokes `dispatch_request`, so each request gets an instance of the subclass while the registry still only sees a function.

`MethodView` extends this pattern. `http_method_funcs` (`src/flask/views.py:11`) declares the recognized lowercase HTTP method names. During subclass creation, `__init_subclass__` (`165`) inspects the class body and records which methods are present, so the view advertises only the HTTP methods it can handle. At request time, `MethodView.dispatch_request` (`182`) reads the active request method and calls the matching class attribute such as `get` or `post`.

## Key symbols
- `View` (`src/flask/views.py:16`): base class for single-dispatch class-based views.
- `dispatch_request` (`78`): the method subclasses implement.
- `as_view` (`86`): converts a view class into a routable function.
- `MethodView` (`138`): base class that dispatches to method-named handlers.
- `__init_subclass__` (`165`): computes allowed methods from the subclass definition.
- `dispatch_request` (`182`): routes the current request to `get`, `post`, etc.

## Gotchas
`MethodView`'s allowed methods are decided in `__init_subclass__` (`165`) from the class body. Adding an HTTP handler to an instance after the class has been created will not make that method routable, because the dispatch table was already fixed at class creation.

## Overview
`src/flask/json/tag.py` implements the tagged JSON serializer used for data that must survive JSON encoding with extra type information. `TaggedJSONSerializer` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:219`) transforms Python values through registered tags and then converts the tagged form to or from JSON. The module is used by Flask's session machinery so session contents can include values beyond plain strings, numbers, lists, and dictionaries.

## Why it exists
JSON natively handles only a small set of types. Cookies and secure sessions need to round-trip values such as bytes, UUIDs, datetimes, tuples, and Markup objects without silently changing their type. A separate tag layer records type information inside the JSON structure, allowing `dumps` and `loads` to restore the original Python object while the serialized data remains valid JSON.

## How it works
The base tag contract is `JSONTag` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:60`), whose subclasses implement `check`, `to_json`, and `to_python`. Built-in tags cover dictionaries (`TagDict`, `93`), pass-through dictionaries (`PassDict`, `119`), tuples (`TagTuple`, `133`), pass-through lists (`PassList`, `147`), bytes (`TagBytes`, `159`), Markup (`TagMarkup`, `173`), UUIDs (`TagUUID`, `191`), and datetimes (`TagDateTime`, `205`). The `TaggedJSONSerializer` constructor (`249`) starts with these tags, and `register` (`256`) is the extension point for custom tag classes.

Encoding begins with `tag` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:289`), which walks values, asks each tag whether it matches, and nests tagged output. Decoding is the inverse: `untag` (`297`) and the internal `_untag_scan` (`309`) detect tagged markers and call the appropriate `to_python`. Public operations are `dumps` (`321`) and `loads` (`325`), which hand the tagged representation to and from standard JSON.

## Key symbols
- `JSONTag` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:60`): base interface for all tags.
- `TaggedJSONSerializer` (`219`): central registry and recursive encoder/decoder.
- `register` (`256`): adds or replaces a tag class.
- `tag` (`289`) / `untag` (`297`): recursive conversion between Python objects and tagged JSON.
- `dumps` (`321`) / `loads` (`325`): public JSON-facing wrappers.

## Gotchas
The tag and untag transformations are paired. Each built-in tag has matching `to_json` and `to_python` methods, and changing one side without the other will make previously serialized session data unreadable. Custom tags registered through `register` (`256`) must also implement both directions for full round-tripping.
